articles.title: La broma del Pedro Sánchez más "jugón" a costa de los Knicks de la NBA y el Mundial de España
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez, presidente del Gobierno de España y secretario general del PSOE, se acuerda del triunfo de Knicks en la NBA y de España en el Mundial en un discurso en Nueva York ante el mediático alcalde Zohran Mamdani.
articles.body: Pedro Sánchez, presidente del Gobierno de España y secretario general del PSOE, se acuerda del triunfo de Knicks en la NBA y de España en el Mundial en un discurso en Nueva York ante el mediático alcalde Zohran Mamdani. "Los Knicks ganaron el campeonato de la NBA. Y España ganó el Mundial. Así que quizás, alcalde, sólo queda una cosa por demostrar: que las políticas progresistas también pueden ganar el futuro", dijo Pedro Sánchez en el acto denominado Construir una economía para la mayoría. Desde la cuenta oficial del PSOE en Instagram destacaron que "hoy Pedro Sánchez está jugón".

articles.title: La española Awa Fam cierra su primera temporada en la WNBA con récord de puntos
articles.standfirst: Awa FAm anotó 22 puntos, la cifra más alta de su carrera, en el último partido de su temporada de novata
articles.summary: Awa FAm anotó 22 puntos, la cifra más alta de su carrera, en el último partido de su temporada de novata
articles.body: Awa Fam cerró su primera temporada en la WNBA, en la que ha promediado 10,3 puntos y 5,9 rebotes por partido tras haber sido elegida en el número tres del 'draft' por las Seattle Storm. La española tuvo un adiós agridulce a su primera temporada, con un récord de puntos -22- en una nueva derrota de Seattle por 91-103 frente a las Dallas Wings. Fam firmó 22 puntos, 7 rebotes y un tapón en este, el último partido de la temporada de las Storm, que no disputarán los 'playoff'. Fam llegó a la WNBA con la temporada empezada, después de acordar con las Storm terminar la campaña con el Valencia Basket. Unas semanas antes, había hecho historia al convertirse en la española seleccionada más arriba en un 'draft' de la WNBA. La valenciana ha disputado 37 partidos, 26 como titular, para una media de 10,3 puntos, 5,9 rebotes, 1,8 asistencias, 0,8 robos y 0,8 tapones por encuentro en su temporada de 'rookie'. Fam cierra la temporada con 380 puntos y 220 rebotes. Con 20 años, la de Santa Pola se ha convertido en la jugadora más joven de la historia de la WNBA en alcanzar los 50 triples y los 200 rebotes, en una liga en la que la mayoría de jugadoras llegan después su paso por la universidad. Sin embargo, la temporada de las Storm ha dejado mucho que desear. En plena reconstrucción, Seattle termina la campaña como el último equipo de la liga, con un balance de 8-36, por debajo incluso de las dos franquicias debutantes: Toronto Tempo y Portland Fire.

articles.title: El Real Madrid inicia la reconquista
articles.standfirst: Los blancos, campeones en 2023 y finalistas en cuatro de las últimas cinco ediciones, abren en Dubái una Euroliga en la que quieren volver a reinar con Pedro Martínez
articles.summary: Los blancos, campeones en 2023 y finalistas en cuatro de las últimas cinco ediciones, abren en Dubái una Euroliga en la que quieren volver a reinar con Pedro Martínez
articles.body: El Real Madrid estrena su Euroliga en el Coca-Cola Arena de Dubái (18.00 horas) con un objetivo que va mucho más allá de este primer partido: volver a levantar el trofeo. El equipo blanco ha sido finalista en 2022, campeón en 2023, finalista otra vez en 2024 y, más recientemente, en 2026. Con una plantilla reforzada y renovadas ambiciones, el Madrid quiere recuperar el trono europeo. Ya le toca volver a reinar. El primer capítulo de esa reconquista es ante el mismo rival al que derrotó hace seis días en las semis de la novedosa SuperCup de la Euroliga. El Dubai Basketball puso contra las cuerdas al Madrid, que remontó 16 puntos y acabó ganando 95-98 en la prórroga. "Deberíamos ser capaces de estar ya preparados desde el minuto uno. Luego estar agresivos en defensa y la lucha por el rebote va a ser muy importante. Ellos son bastante físicos y el rebote es donde más se puede ver", analiza Pedro Martínez, que se estrena en la Euroliga como entrenador madridista. Ahora el escenario cambia y también la exigencia: comienza la Euroliga y cada partido cuenta en el camino hacia Abu Dabi, sede de la próxima Final Four. "Empezamos de cero, sin pensar demasiado en lo anterior. Sabemos que es una competición tremendamente difícil para todo el mundo. Son 38 partidos y todos los equipos tienen momentos buenos y momentos malos a lo largo del año. Se vio la temporada pasada que con tantísimos partidos es muy difícil mantener un nivel muy alto para todos y hay que estar mentalmente muy preparado", explica Pedro Martínez. El Madrid ha aprovechado estos días en los emiratos, donde se quedó tras ganar la SuperCup, para trabajar sin viajes de por medio y llega con todos sus efectivos salvo Usman Garuba, lesionado de larga duración, y Nick Smith Jr., que viajó pero aún no ha sido dado de alta en la máxima competición continental. Dubai, reforzado con Shengelia, Okobo, Mintz, Blossomgame, Diakite y el recién llegado Walkup, será la primera prueba de verdad. Xavi Pascual ha construido un equipo para competir con los grandes, cosa que intentará este jueves pese a la baja del exmadridista Dzanan Musa, y la duda de Prepelic, otro ex. Sí estará Petrusev.

articles.title: Gregg Popovich se casa con 77 años con la ex de su entrenador asistente durante 17 temporadas
articles.standfirst: Gregg Popovich y Mike Budenholzer ganaron juntos cuatro anillos de la NBA con los San Antonio Spurs
articles.summary: Gregg Popovich y Mike Budenholzer ganaron juntos cuatro anillos de la NBA con los San Antonio Spurs
articles.body: Gregg Popovich, uno de los mejores entrenadores de la historia de la NBA, se ha casado con 77 años. El mítico técnico de los San Antonio Spurs, tal y como adelanta TMZ (tuvo acceso a la licencia de matrimonio), contrajo matrimonio con Mary Barth Budenholzer, la exmujer de su entrenador asistente Mike Budenholzer. Los recién casados intercambiaron sus anillos de boda el 16 de septiembre en Texas... según la licencia de matrimonio registrada en el condado de Bexar (Texas). Mike Budenholzer trabajó como entrenador asistente a las órdenes de Gregg Popovich en los Spurs durante 17 temporadas —de 1996 a 2013— antes de marcharse para asumir el puesto de entrenador jefe de los Atlanta Hawks. Juntos ganaron campeonatos de la NBA con los San Antonio Spurs Mike y Mary se divorciaron discretamente en 2016 y en 2018 murió Erin Popovich, la primera esposa de Pop.

articles.title: El KO, el juego que pone a prueba a los aficionados: elige un ganador, sobrevive y no podrás repetir equipo
articles.standfirst: El nuevo juego de acb Play obliga a elegir un ganador diferente cada jornada y premia al último superviviente con tres fines de semana de baloncesto
articles.summary: El nuevo juego de acb Play obliga a elegir un ganador diferente cada jornada y premia al último superviviente con tres fines de semana de baloncesto
articles.body: La Liga Endesa estrena un juego en el que cada jornada puede ser la última. El KO llega a acb Play con una mecánica sencilla y exigente: elegir un equipo ganador cada semana y sobrevivir. Si pierde, mueres. Si gana, sigues vivo, aunque ese equipo ya no podrá volver a ser elegido. Una decisión que apenas lleva un minuto puede acompañarte durante toda la semana porque un solo fallo supone la eliminación. Cada participante dispone de una única oportunidad. En cada jornada deberá escoger un equipo que crea que va a ganar su partido. El contador de supervivientes irá bajando semana tras semana hasta el término de la primera vuelta. El reto pasa por superar las 17 jornadas y para conseguirlo habrá que acertar 17 ganadores diferentes sin cometer un solo error. Con 18 equipos disponibles, llegará un momento en el que tocará confiar incluso en ese rival que nunca elegirías en otras circunstancias. El último superviviente optará a un premio único. El ganador podrá elegir tres partidos de la segunda vuelta y vivir tres fines de semana con viaje, hotel y entradas para un partido para dos personas. El plazo para apuntarse termina el sábado 26 de septiembre a las 18:00h, coincidiendo con el comienzo de la Liga Endesa 2026-27. A partir de ahí, cada elección marcará la continuidad en el juego. El mecanismo se sostiene sobre dos normas. La primera obliga a elegir cada jornada un equipo al que el participante vea ganador: si acierta, continúa; si falla, queda eliminado. La segunda añade toda la estrategia. Cada equipo solo puede utilizarse una vez durante las 17 jornadas. Escoger a uno en la primera fecha significa renunciar a él durante el resto del juego, por muy favorable que resulte alguno de sus siguientes partidos. Hay 18 equipos para 17 jornadas, así que prácticamente todos tendrán que entrar en los planes tarde o temprano. El juego incluye además un comodín. Cada usuario podrá utilizarlo una sola vez y tendrá de plazo hasta el final del tercer cuarto del partido elegido. Si el encuentro se tuerce y la apuesta pinta mal, podrá activar ese recurso y salvar la jornada. Una vez gastado, desaparece cualquier margen de seguridad para lo que quede de primera vuelta. Una estrategia para sobrevivir 17 jornadas El KO obliga a mirar el partido inmediato y, al mismo tiempo, todo el calendario. No basta con localizar al favorito de cada jornada. También hay que decidir cuándo gastar cada equipo, medir qué opciones pueden aparecer más adelante y administrar un comodín que solo ofrece una vida extra. Guardar demasiado a un conjunto puede dejarlo sin utilidad; utilizarlo demasiado pronto puede echarse de menos semanas después. Un solo fallo, en cualquier jornada, termina la partida. No hay una segunda oportunidad más allá de ese comodín ni posibilidad de recuperar un equipo ya utilizado. Durante 17 jornadas, el participante tendrá que combinar conocimiento de la Liga Endesa, estrategia y sangre fría mientras el contador de supervivientes se reduce semana tras semana.

articles.title: Legendary Lakers PA announcer Lawrence Tanter dies at 76
articles.summary: Longtime Lakers public address announcer Lawrence Tanter has died at age 76, the team announced.
articles.body: Longtime Lakers public address announcer Lawrence Tanter has died at age 76, the team announced. Tanter had been the Lakers’ public address announcer through the 2025- 26 season. The team announced in June that Tanter retired from the position but would remain with the organization as its special adviser for game presentation. “We are deeply saddened to share the news of the passing of legendary Lakers public address announcer Lawrence Tanter,’’ the team announced Wednesday night. “For 43 years, LT’s voice served as the soundtrack to Lakers games at the arena. He will be remembered as a cherished member of the Lakers family.’’ Tanter’s tenure with the Lakers spanned 10 NBA championships, 16 Western Conference titles and some of the most successful eras in franchise history. During the NBA’s pandemic-era bubble in 2020, Tanter recorded game introductions from his home studio to help recreate the familiar atmosphere of Lakers basketball. Tanter was also a disc jockey for Los Angeles-area radio stations KJLH, KTWV and KKJZ.

articles.title: LeBron James’ longtime business partner Maverick Carter clashes with ex Crystal Streets over daughter's child support
articles.summary: LeBron James’ longtime business partner and childhood friend Maverick Carter is facing a court battle with his ex-partner Crystal Streets over child
articles.body: LeBron James’ longtime business partner and childhood friend Maverick Carter is facing a court battle with his ex-partner Crystal Streets over child support payments. Court documents show Carter has asked a judge to stop the $25,000 monthly payments he currently makes for their daughter.Carter says their 18-year-old daughter lives at a full-time boarding school, whose costs he pays in full. He argues that Streets has little “meaningful” custodial time because their daughter lives away at school. Streets disagrees and wants the payments to continue until their daughter graduates.Maverick Carter asks court to end $25K monthly child support paymentsAccording to court documents seen by TMZ, MaverickCarter is seeking to reduce his monthly child support obligation from $25,000 to $0. He says the request is not an attempt to avoid supporting his daughter. Instead, he argues that he pays directly for everything she needs.Carter’s legal team also pointed to the fact that their daughter turned 18 in July. He argued that the court no longer had jurisdiction over custody matters involving her after she reached adulthood.The businessman is represented in the case by high-profile family law attorney Laura Wasser.Streets has challenged Carter’s request. She claims Carter is worth more than $100 million and should continue paying support while their daughter finishes school.She has asked the court to increase the monthly payment to $35,000. Streets also claims that she and Carter agreed to the higher amount in 2024. However, she says the agreement was never finalized because of the California wildfires.Streets has also rejected Carter’s description of her role in their daughter’s life. She says she continues to provide emotional support and remains involved in her daughter’s day-to-day needs.According to the court documents, Streets says she also coordinates travel and provides for her daughter even though she is currently living at boarding school.The case also includes alleged emails between Carter and Streets. One email, dated December 28, 2025, appears to have been sent by Carter to his former partner.In the message, he allegedly wrote, “Dealing with you is the only thing bad about my life, and I’ll be soooo happy when it’s over.”The dispute came before a judge at a hearing on September 15. Streets argued that Carter’s child support payments should not be terminated.Carter disagreed and maintained his position that the payments should end.The court has not yet issued a final ruling on the dispute. For now, Carter’s child support obligations have been suspended for three months while the court considers the arguments made by both sides.The legal battle comes as Carter remains widely known for his longtime relationship with LeBron James. articles.title: Ranking the NBA's Best Young Cores Right Now
articles.summary: Young NBA talent is, by its very nature, exciting.
articles.body:
Young NBA talent is, by its very nature, exciting.

What feels perhaps different now more than ever, though, is that there doesn't have to be any delay between that excitement and the realization of what it can become.

While young hoopers often tantalize for what they might become tomorrow, some of them are genuine juggernauts today. You might notice, then, some direct overlap between this conversation of the Association's best young cores and general power rankings of teams as a whole.

There are, of course, still some "They got next" rebuilders who are flooded with youth but impacted by all the uncertainty that so often comes along with it. There just also happens to be some "They got now" powerhouses who can go (and have gone) toe-to-toe with the top-ranked heavyweights in the entire hoops world.

Speaking of rankings, let's dig into the discussion at hand by sorting the league's best young cores—weighing players in their age-24 seasons or younger—by everything from high-end talent and on-paper production to on-court cohesiveness and long-term potential.

The Hornets pack a powerful 1-2 punch with their young core led by 21-year-old Kon Knueppel (silver medalist in last season's Rookie of the Year voting) and 23-year-old Brandon Miller (20.2 points on 43.5/38.3/89.2 shooting in 2025-26). They just don't have many known contributors beyond them. Sion James looks solid but not special, and there are questions about first-round rookies Hannes Steinbach (perimeter utility) and Christian Anderson Jr. (lack of size and strength).

It's tempting to reserve Dallas a top-five spot here by virtue of rostering reigning Rookie of the Year winner Cooper Flagg alone. It just feels hard to justify that when he is sort of on an island with Dereck Lively II struggling to stay on the court, and the NBA odometers showing goose eggs for first-round rookies Morez Johnson Jr. and Sergio de Larrea.

If these rankings went six spots deep, the Grizzlies would've made the cut. And some will argue they still belong in the top five given Cameron Boozer's polish, Cedric Coward's production and Zach Edey's flashes. That said, if Boozer winds up closer to good than great, Memphis might be missing a true needle-mover, with Coward perhaps bumping into his ceiling soon (he's already 23) and Edey facing agility limitations.

It should be obvious pretty early into the season whether the Jazz are ranked too high, too low or just right. Because, honestly, things could go just about any direction from here.

Plenty will depend on the readiness and impact of No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson. He was, in the eyes of many, the best prospect in his class. ESPN's Jeremy Woo put Peterson atop his 2026 draft big board and called him "the most gifted scorer in the draft," "a ramarkable long-range shotmaker" and "a strong athlete with good size for a ball-handler."

If Peterson gets back the explosiveness and playmaking he showcased late in his prep career, he could be a full-fledged, two-way star. He's also far from the only swing factor in Salt Lake City. There are also eyeballs on Keyonte George and the sustainability of his third-year breakout, a possible sophomore leap for scoring swingman Ace Bailey and the developmental hurdles cleared (or plowed into) by Isaiah Collier, Brice Sensabaugh and Kyle Filipowski.

A touch more certainty is needed to slot these young Jazz any higher, in other words, but ample potential remains within that unpredictability. A banner year from this bunch could vault it into a top-three ranking and perhaps even help Utah crash the playoff party.

The Rockets may not be first to mind when thinking of a young team, but they aren't lacking for young talent.

Alperen Şengün, who turned 24 in July, is already a two-time All-Star who flourishes as a 6'11" offensive hub. Amen Thompson, who will be 24 in January, is an all-purpose defensive stopper and athletic 6'7" playmaker. Throw in 23-year-old Jabari Smith Jr. (functionally a 6'11" three-and-D forward) and 22-year-old Reed Sheppard (a sharpshooter with some creation chops), and this is a core than shine on either end of the court.

Is it lacking quantity? Maybe, but quality is always the true aim, and Houston has that in spades. Şengün is an established star, and Thompson might be a couple offensive improvements away from superstardom. Smith is, at worst, a rock-solid starter, and Sheppard's best-case scenarios let the imagination run wild .

Houston's win-right-now timeline doesn't leave a ton of wiggle room for growing pains, but these players have all handled the pressure in ways that makes you forget they might all have big developmental jumps still in front of them. That is a scary thought—well, it is anywhere outside of Space City, at least.

This should not be fair. A team this successful—back-to-back seasons with NBA-best win totals, six series triumphs (including the 2025 Finals) in this stretch—should not have this much young talent at its disposal. Having Sam Presti calling the shots, it seems, is no less than a real-life cheat code.

OKC can point toward both star power and strength in numbers as reasons behind its bronze medal here. Chet Holmgren just captured third-team All-NBA and first-team All-Defensive honors. Cason Wallace, who has yet to hold a full-time starting role, just snagged an All-Defensive second-team spot. If Ajay Mitchell's rising star appears cloudy at all, it's only due to the ridiculous depth of this roster.

Speaking of which, that's merely the foundation of this celebrated young core. Because there's been no mention yet of slithery shot-maker Jared McCain, nor of sturdy and stretch-y (and savvy) center Jaylin Williams. Never mind the many first-rounders who have hardly played (Nikola Topić) or have yet to debut (Aday Mara, Bennett Stirtz, Thomas Sorber).

This is, in technical economic terms, an absurd embarassment of riches. And yet, the core is still confined to merely the No. 3 spot due to the wealth of ascending (and, in many ways, established) talent still in front of it.

Some might quibble over Washington's placement, since this core lacks the league-wide accolades of the few right behind it. Where the Wizards can counter, though, is with the documented growth of their group already and the vast untapped potential still ahead of it.

They are overloaded with recent first-round picks to the point that the idea of listing them all carries the worry of not having enough digital ink to cover the lot: AJ Dybantsa (No. 1 in 2026), Tre Johnson (No. 6 in 2025), Will Riley (No. 21 in 2025), Alex Sarr (No. 2 in 2024), Bub Carrington (No. 14 in 2024), Kyshawn George (No. 24 in 2024) and Bilal Coulibaly (No. 7 in 2023). Tristan Vukčević (No. 42 in 2023) isn't offically part of that group, but he might be a first-rounder in a re-draft.

You know what that core all has in common, besides the draft pedigree? They're all under the age of 24. And save for Dybantsa, a possible Tracy McGrady clone , they all have encouraging track records, too. The core kind of has everything: ignitable shooting, slippery shot-creation, electric slashing, defensive versatility, quick-strike scoring.

In fact, is has more (by quantity) than even the No. 1 ranked core on this list. It's just missing a legitimate superstar, which is kind of a big deal when our gold medalists happen to have a 22-year-old pushing for best-player-on-the-planet status and two 21-and-under sidekicks showing star trajectories of their own.

The quartet featured above—all age 22 or under—just all filled regular playoff rotation minutes for a 62-win NBA Finalist. Victor Wembanyama served as the centerpiece, Stephon Castle joined him in the starting five, Dylan Harper arguably deserved a starting spot and Carter Bryant drew one marquee matchup after another .

San Antonio may not have much else for the purpose of this exercise—it's wait-and-see with first-round rookies Jayden Quaintance and Tarris Reed Jr.—but it doesn't need anything else. Such is the luxury of snagging three consecutive top-four picks and turning them into Wembanyama (No. 1 in 2023), Castle (No. 4 in 2024) and Harper (No. 2 in 2025).

Their ages suggest they could be years away from maxing out their potential. Incredibly, the eye test tells a similar tale. Wembanyama, as great as he is, is still finding his go-to scoring strength (as a 51-percent shooting 25-point scorer). Castle's jumper remains a work in progress. Harper could stand to up his distance shooting and playmaking. Carter is ridiculously bounce, but he's also basically a blank slate on offense.

Yet, even while acknowledging all of the improvements still needed, this looks like the foundation of a multi-time championship dynasty. Considering how it has fared so far and how much more it could do with a few developmental successes, that trophy count could start climbing as soon as this season.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: How will playoff seeding shake out for the Golden State Valkyries, Las Vegas Aces, Indiana Fever and Washington Mystics?
articles.summary: On the final day of the WNBA regular season, four playoff seeds remain unsettled.
articles.body:
Following Wednesday's WNBA games, four of eight playoff seeds are now settled.

After the Minnesota Lynx , with an (unwanted?) assist from the Portland Fire , locked down the No. 1 seed on Tuesday, the Atlanta Dream earned the No. 4 seed and homecourt advantage in the first round with a second-straight win over the now-official No. 8-seed New York Liberty . With New York's loss, the Dallas Wings secured the No. 7 seed with their win over the Seattle Storm .

That leaves the No. 2 seed, No. 3 seed, No. 5 seed and No. 6 seed still undetermined. Here's the current state of the standings, with asterisks denoting the seeds that are finalized:

If all of the Golden State Valkyries , Las Vegas Aces, Indiana Fever and Washington Mystics win, things will remain as is. That outcome probably should be the expectation.

However, let's take a closer look at the stakes and scenarios facing the Valkyries, Aces, Fever and Mystics. In the comments, be sure to give your predictions.

Golden State Valkyries vs. Los Angeles Sparks (10 p.m. ET, WNBA League Pass)

The Valkyries are the opponent for the final game of Nneka Ogwumike 's WNBA career.

While a loss would slightly better the Sparks' lottery odds, the team has appeared to prioritize competing with the kind of class Nneka demonstrated throughout her career—they've won their last three games over fellow lottery-bound teams—over any potential percentage bump in lottery balls.

If the Sparks are motivated to send off Nneka with a win, the Valkyries might have a more challenging game than anticipated. They enter with a clean injury report, and plenty of incentive to clinch the No. 2 seed.

With a win, they would set up a first round series against the No. 7-seed Wings. Golden State swept the season series against Dallas, winning the three games by 11 points, 18 points and eight points.

That said, will the Valkyries view avoiding injury as even more valuable?

On Wednesday, the Liberty opted to rest Breanna Stewart , with head coach Chris DeMarco suggesting the decision was "just precautionary with some soreness." (Or, New York wanted the first round series against Minnesota, rather than Golden State or Vegas?)

Unfortunately for the Liberty, their precaution with Stewie was proven particularly smart when Jonquel Jones suffered an ankle injury after stepping on a fan's foot. She was ruled out for the remainder of the game. Early indications are that it is not serious enough to sideline her for the playoffs, with DeMarco sharing that she was "in good spirits" after the game.

Atlanta also experienced an injury scare when Sabrina Ionescu 's errant arm bar hit Angel Reese in the face, sending her back to the locker room and requiring her to miss the start of the second half; Angel eventually returned to the game.

Those plays, however, might be on the mind of Golden State head coach Natalie Nakase as she manages her team's final game.

Las Vegas Aces vs. Phoenix Mercury (10 p.m. ET, USA Network/CNBC)

The WNBA schedule makers thought they were cooking by scheduling a rematch of the 2025 WNBA Finals as the final game for the Aces and Phoenix Mercury.

Of course, when the Mercury saw the Aces across the way on opening day, they delivered what turned out to be their very best performance of the season, blowing out the defending champs on their homecourt. Might Phoenix bookend their season with a similar showing? (Such a circumstance, however, might be more torturous than thrilling for Mercury fans who have had to witness a lot of disappointment between the opener and finale.)

If the Valkyries win, the Aces are stuck in the No. 3 seed, regardless of what happens.

So, I would expect head coach Becky Hammon's hoodied assistants to be closely monitoring the score in LA. If the Valkyries establish a lead, there's no reason to put any extra miles on the Big 3 of A'ja Wilson, Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young . Conversely, if the Sparks are giving it their all for Nneka, the Aces might be motivated to push for the win.

As I noted yesterday , Dallas, the No. 7 seed, had an edge over Vegas this season, possibly incentivizing the Aces to avoid the No. 2 seed.

A decision also could be influenced by which team ends up in the No. 6 seed, as the results of Fever-Lynx should be settled by tip off in Phoenix, if not soon after. Vegas lost the season series to Indiana 1-2, with that one win requiring a near miracle, and won the season over Washington 2-1, although both wins were hard-fought.

Considering the Fever gave the Aces their toughest series during last season's title run, I could see them gunning for the No. 2 seed if Indiana falls to No. 6. But again, that's only possible if it appears Golden State is going to lose to Los Angeles .

Indiana Fever vs. Minnesota Lynx (8 p.m. ET, USA Network)

Even with the No. 1 seed locked up, Olivia Miles is the only rotational regular on the Lynx listed on the injury report.

That means the four starters that head coach Cheryl Reeve benched for the second half of Tuesday's loss in Indiana— Napheesa Collier , Kayla McBride , Courtney Williams and Natasha Howard —will at least start this game, barring a late change to the injury report.

While the motivation behind Reeve's move on Tuesday can be debated as truly about rest, a statement about the starters' play or a possibly failed attempt at playoff matchup manipulation, it would be surprising if any of those four play significant minutes.

The Lynx's absence of incentives should make this a relatively easy Fever win, which would keep them in the No. 5 seed and set up a first-round rematch with the No. 4-seed Dream.

However, Minnesota's deeper reserves, likely aware that they're going to see little, if any, playing time in the playoffs, could cause Indy some troubles. For such players, this is a perfect proving ground for their next contract, whether for an overseas team or next season in the W. They're going to try their best to make Indiana earn that No. 5 seed.

And, are we sure the Fever want the No. 5 seed?

I think so. As mentioned above, they've given the likely No. 3-seed Aces some problems, but angling to play the defending champs over a Dream group that's never won a playoff series together would be insane.

Chicago Sky vs. Washington Mystics (7:30 p.m. ET, WNBA League Pass)

The Chicago Sky's injury report features five names, with more possibly added before tip off.

Washington can add insult to those injuries: Giving the Sky one more L would provide a final lottery-ball boost for the Mystics, as Washington owns Chicago's 2027 first-round pick.

However, I would expect injury avoidance to be DC's top priority, as they are dependent on a Fever loss to escape the No. 6 seed.

Whether they end up as the No. 5 seed or No. 6 seed, the Mystics should enter the playoffs pressure-free as ahead-of-schedule overachievers, which should make the Dream, Aces or Valkyries wary if they end up with Washington on the other side.

articles.title: Olivia Miles is our Rookie of the Year. But who else stood out in a deep WNBA class?
articles.summary: As the playoff picture is finally coming into focus, it’s fitting that the final seeds won’t be settled until the last day of the season. You know what’s not...
articles.body:
As the playoff picture is finally coming into focus, it's fitting that the final seeds won't be settled until the last day of the season.

You know what's not being left until the last day of the season? The Athletic 's experts taking stock of the league and making decisions on year-end awards.

We unveiled our choices for Most Improved Player and Coach of the Year on Wednesday. Now, we continue with our Rookie of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year Award, and Friday, we'll showcase our MVP and All-WNBA teams.

Our experts Annie Costabile, Brian Hamilton, Chantel Jennings and Sabreena Merchant explain their votes.

Olivia Miles was the unanimous pick, and that's no surprise. With her outstanding play, the No. 2 pick in the 2026 WNBA Draft played her way into the MVP debate and ran away with the ROY award.

The more contested selections were those who followed Miles. Azzi Fudd, the No. 1 pick in this year's draft, averaged 13 points a game and started 24 of 30 games for the Dallas Wings , earning her the second-place nod, and a three-way tie for third rounds out an exclusively guard-occupied top group of rookies.

Here is the list of rookies who finished in the top 20 for win shares this season: Miles. Here are some players who had fewer win shares than Miles: Allisha Gray , Caitlin Clark , Alyssa Thomas , Angel Reese . It's bonkers, the debut season Miles had. The calls past that were difficult, though, considering Taylor's surprise breakout with the Chicago Sky and Kiki Rice starting and finishing strong, around an injury-related slump in the middle. Fudd didn't finish the season, but she was an emerging two-way standout for Dallas. — Brian Hamilton

Miles is my MVP; that's how good of a rookie she has been. Fudd was a quality starter on a winning team while she was healthy, leading the Wings in on-off differential. Taylor was buried on the bench for too long, but when she was in the starting lineup, she averaged 15.4 points on 35.3 percent shooting from beyond the arc; more importantly, the struggling Sky had a positive point differential in those minutes. A hat tip to Astier, Rice, Lauren Betts and the Seattle Storm duo of Flau'jae Johnson and Awa Fam, all of whom had seasons worthy of the all-rookie team, but it's a deep class. — Sabreena Merchant

The Rookie of the Year race was not close. Miles became the front-runner before the All-Star break when she carried the Minnesota Lynx to the top of the leaderboard without 2025 MVP runner-up Napheesa Collier . The rookie class this year was more about depth than anything. Between Fudd finding her rhythm in Dallas, Taylor being one of the few bright lights in Chicago, and Astier, Rice and Johnson all showing up as significant contributors for their teams, the 2026 rookie class is in the conversation as one of the deepest. — Annie Costabile

In the WNBA's history, only five players have averaged 19-plus points and six-plus assists over the course of a season: Diana Taurasi, Candace Parker, Caitlin Clark (twice), Jackie Young … and Olivia Miles. Among them, Miles averaged the fewest minutes. With all due respect to the other rookies in this class, only one player was completely un-rookie-like and instead played like someone who's putting herself in the same category as the DTs and CPs of the world. — Chantel Jennings

Angel Reese was the only player among our top three who appeared on each of our ballots, earning the top nod from three of our voters. But it was a tightly contested race beyond the top spot, as several players' defensive contributions were recognized.

Unlike the ROY, the DPOY battle spanned positions, which — rightfully so — indicates the deep defensive versatility in the WNBA, a near-necessity now for players, whether they initially get in their stance in the paint or on the perimeter.

Also receiving votes: Sonia Citron , Washington Mystics; Veronica Burton, Golden State Valkyries.

As someone who was never mistaken for an adequate defender on a basketball court, I'm a little hesitant to make appraisals here. So I'll just rely on numbers. Reese finished first in total rebounds, third in defensive rebounds, third in steals, first in defensive win shares and fourth in defensive rating. She can guard all five spots on the floor. Reese is a massive asset for one of the league's top defensive outfits. — Hamilton

Entering the final stretch of regular-season games, Reese was the league leader in defensive win shares, third in defensive rebound percentage, tied for third in defensive boards and tied for first in steal percentage (among players averaging at least five rebounds per game). Among high-usage players, no one has had a better on-off differential for defensive team rating. On top of that, what the stats don't show is her versatility to guard all five positions and her activity that causes deflections, misdirections and turnovers. — Jennings

Williams has been the best defender on the WNBA's top-rated defensive team, but Reese's numbers don't lie. Her stats are impressive, and her defensive prowess is best measured by her overall impact. The Atlanta Dream have the fourth-best defensive rating (103.9) in the league, but it improves to 99.3 when Reese is on the court. — Costabile

Citron is consistently tasked with defending the opponent's best player, and she does it better than any other perimeter defender in the league. Among players who have contested at least 100 shots by All-Stars, Citron allows the lowest effective field goal percentage and the lowest expected shot quality. Put plainly, she forces the best players into the worst possible shots. In a league that emphasizes freedom of movement and is becoming increasingly friendly toward offense from the perimeter, the job of a wing stopper has never been more difficult. Citron still gets it done. — Merchant
authors: Annie Costabile, Brian Hamilton and more

articles.title: Lawrence Tanter, Legendary Lakers PA Announcer, Dies at Age 76
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers announced Thursday that longtime public-address announcer Lawrence Tanter died at the age of 76.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers announced Thursday that longtime public-address announcer Lawrence Tanter died at the age of 76.

Tanter had spent 43 years as the Lakers' PA announcer, dating back to the 1980s, which was a decade that saw L.A. win five championships.

According to ESPN's Dave McMenamin , Tanter retired in June after suffering a stroke and missing the Lakers' final six regular-season home games and the playoffs late in the 2025-26 campaign.

Just before he entered hospice care last month, Tanter texted McMenamin, "Quote me. It's been a blessing."

Originally from Chicago, Tanter spent many years as a DJ on jazz radio stations in addition to his role with the Lakers, per McMenamin.

Over the course of his long and successful career, Tanter was with the Lakers organization for 10 of their 18 championships, including the most recent one in 2020.

articles.title: WNBA Playoff Picture 2026, Updated Bracket Scenarios and Standings Before Final Games
articles.summary: The final day of the WNBA regular season will decide the playoff seeding of four of the eight playoff participants.
articles.body:
The final day of the WNBA regular season will decide the playoff seeding of four of the eight playoff participants.

The Minnesota Lynx are locked into the No. 1 seed. They will face the New York Liberty, who were confirmed as the No. 8 seed after their loss to the Atlanta Dream on Wednesday. Atlanta landed the No. 4 seed with the victory.

The Dallas Wings secured the No. 7 seed with their Wednesday win over the Seattle Storm.

The Nos. 2, 3, 5 and 6 seeds will be determined during Thursday's five-game slate. Four of those contests will have an impact on the playoff standings.

A'ja Wilson and the Las Vegas Aces will try to pry the No. 2 seed away from the Golden State Valkyries, but they'll need some help to do so.

Caitlin Clark and the Indiana Fever need a win in Minnesota to remain in the No. 5 position ahead of the Washington Mystics.

The equation is simple for the Golden State Valkyries and Indiana Fever on Thursday.

Golden State needs to beat the Los Angeles Sparks to confirm its spot as the No. 2 seed in the postseason bracket.

A Golden State loss combined with a Las Vegas Aces win over the Phoenix Mercury slots the Aces into the No. 2 seed on the head-to-head tiebreaker.

Indiana needs a second straight win over the Minnesota Lynx to lock into the No. 5 seed.

The Fever beat the Lynx, who have nothing to play for on Thursday, by 19 points on Tuesday.

The Washington Mystics must beat the Chicago Sky and have the Fever lose to the Lynx to jump into the No. 5 seed. The Mystics won the regular-season series with Indiana, so they would jump ahead on tiebreaker if they finish on the same record.

All four WNBA first-round series start on Sunday. The opening round is a best-of-three series, the semifinals are best-of-five and the WNBA Finals are best-of-seven.

articles.title: Final WNBA Power Rankings Ahead of 2026 Playoffs
articles.summary: There's only one day remaining in the 2026 WNBA regular season, and while there are still plenty of seeding implications on the line, let's run through our final power rankings ahead of the postseason.
articles.body:
There's only one day remaining in the 2026 WNBA regular season, and while there are still plenty of seeding implications on the line, let's run through our final power rankings ahead of the postseason.

The most interesting thing from this season was just how quickly the top eight teams separated themselves from everyone else. In fact, the gap between No. 1 and No. 8 in the standings is smaller than the gap between No. 8 and No. 9, which has basically never been the case before in league history.

These rankings are a mix of giving teams their flowers for their regular-season success while also projecting how they will translate to a playoff setting. For example, Golden State isn't in our top two despite having the best record since the start of July.

Seattle's 2026 season was always going to be a rollercoaster given how young their core is. The Storm finished with the league's worst record and, in the process, became the worst clutch team in WNBA history, winning just two of their 18 clutch games.

The next step is finding an elite passer to pair with Dominique Malonga, Awa Fam and Flau'jae Johnson. Seattle should have a top five pick in the 2027 draft, along with plenty of cap space to continue building around that young talent.

There's only one game remaining for Connecticut before the franchise moves to Houston next season. There weren't many wins in 2026, but there are still some young players to be excited about, most notably 22-year-old guard Leïla Lacan, who profiles as a high-level secondary ball-handler who can take on tough defensive assignments.

Also, keep an eye on Connecticut against Toronto tonight in the ultimate tank bowl. If the Sun win, the two teams will have to split the top lottery odds—that's the difference between a 29.5 and 35 percent chance at USC's JuJu Watkins (assuming she declares).

On June 11, Toronto was 7-5. Then Kiki Rice missed 16 games with an ankle sprain, while Brittney Sykes missed 18 games with a foot injury. At that point, their playoff chances were completely out of reach.

Even if Toronto had stayed healthy, though, it's hard to see this team making the postseason given their struggles against the best teams. The Tempo finished 1-25 against playoff teams, with their lone win coming against New York two months ago.

Looking ahead, their biggest needs are rim protection and athleticism across the board. Toronto's 116.1 defensive rating is the worst in WNBA history.

Chicago invested a crazy amount of long-term money and traded a valuable future first-round pick last offseason with the hope of making the playoffs for the first time since 2023. But, well, that didn't happen.

Rickea Jackson suffered a torn ACL just four games into the season, Azurá Stevens' shot disappeared, Skylar Diggins wasn't a great fit and there were plenty of other issues with the roster construction beyond that.

On the bright side, Sydney Taylor was an absolute steal in undrafted free agency. She averaged 13.6 points on 42.5 percent shooting from the field and should be on her way to an All-Rookie selection.

Similar to Chicago, Los Angeles made all-in moves last offseason with the goal of making the playoffs, but they were very far away from that and eventually traded Kelsey Plum to Phoenix at the deadline.

We'll see what direction they take after this season, but more likely than not, the Sparks will look to reset and accumulate more young talent.

After making the WNBA Finals just a year ago, the Phoenix Mercury missed the playoffs entirely in 2026. They ranked No. 11 in both offensive and defensive rating, and traded their own 2027 first-round pick for five games of Plum, who is now set to enter unrestricted free agency.

Alyssa Thomas will be 35 next season, while Kahleah Copper just turned 32. Even if Plum returns, what exactly is the ceiling of this team when they don't have many young players or draft picks, either?

Portland entered the season projected to win under 10 games, and almost everyone outside of Oregon assumed they would be the worst team in the league. Instead, they won 17 games and look like a really dangerous team for the future.

Carla Leite is completely unstoppable in ball screens, Bridget Carleton is a very good starting wing, Sarah Ashlee Barker made a massive Year 2 leap before tearing her ACL, Emily Engstler is a legit two-way player and Iyana Martín is coming to the WNBA next season. They also have Alex Sarama, the youngest coach in the league, along with a lottery pick and more cap space than anyone else this offseason.

The Dallas Wings are in the postseason for the first time of the Paige Bueckers era, and we'll learn a lot about where this team is headed from here.

Can you build a contender with Jessica Shepard defensively? What version of Arike Ogunbowale do the Wings get, and is she worth continuing to build around? And will Bueckers show more aggression in a playoff series?

There are plenty of questions to answer, but you can't count out a Bueckers-led team from making things interesting. She shot 49.6 percent on pull-up twos, 41 percent on pull-up threes and 39.7 percent on catch-and-shoot threes, per Synergy Sports. She's just an outrageous shot-maker.

The Washington Mystics shouldn't be this good already. They are the youngest team in WNBA history, rank No. 13 in the league in three-pointers made and committed more turnovers than anyone else. And yet, they always seem to find ways to win basketball games.

Washington makes opposing offenses work for every shot, led by Sonia Citron on the perimeter and Shakira Austin on the interior. They kill teams on the glass, draw a crazy amount of fouls and dominate in the clutch.

Over the last 15 games, though, the Mystics have taken a major step offensively, thanks to Austin's superstar-level play and Georgia Amoore's three-point shooting boosting to 43.2 percent since the All-Star break.

New York's roster looks just as good as any other contender on paper. But as we know, what you actually do on the court matters most, and it's been a very weird year for the Liberty.

They won the season series against Minnesota and Las Vegas, but also lost the season series to Portland and dropped games to Toronto, Seattle and Chicago.

The talent is obviously there, and so is the championship experience. But what version of Sabrina Ionescu do we see in the postseason? And is there enough defense across the perimeter, especially at the point of attack?

The Atlanta Dream have finished the season incredibly well, winning 11 of their last 15 games with a +13.8 net rating—second-best in the league over that stretch.

Angel Reese has become a legitimate Defensive Player of the Year candidate and has been more efficient offensively recently, too. Rhyne Howard has taken an All-WNBA leap this season, while you can always rely on Allisha Gray to be extremely consistent on both ends.

There are still some questions about how Atlanta's style will translate to the playoffs, though. The Dream have the best transition offense in the league because of their ability to force turnovers. But they also have the worst half-court offense among playoff teams at 0.92 points per possession, per Synergy Sports.

If Rhyne Howard and Allisha Gray catch fire from three, Atlanta can beat anyone. If they go cold, like we saw against Indiana last year, they could be a first-round exit again.

The Indiana Fever have the best regular-season offense in WNBA history, scoring 96.7 points per game while shooting 55.2 percent on twos and 39.3 percent from three.

Kelsey Mitchell is the best small-guard scorer this sport has ever seen, Caitlin Clark is a game-breaking playmaker who is now hitting pull-up threes again (43.1% since July 1) and Aliyah Boston has become a legitimate shooter while also being the best defender on the roster.

There's almost no concern offensively. On the other end, though, can this team get enough stops?

Indiana has the worst defensive rating among playoff teams. They don't have enough defensive talent on the perimeter, which forces the defense to constantly be a step behind and scrambling in rotation. That plays a part in their 10-12 record against other playoff teams.

Golden State is basically the exact opposite of Indiana. They win with their No. 1-ranked defense and play a slow brand of basketball offensively, focused on limiting turnovers and firing up threes.

This strategy has been so, so successful in the regular season. Veronica Burton is the best two-way point guard in the league, Gabby Williams is having a career year, Kiah Stokes has been really important defensively after being almost unplayable the last couple years and their depth everywhere is just mind-boggling.

But they do have some questions offensively in a playoff setting, given their No. 8 offensive rating overall and No. 12 in the clutch.

Can Stokes reliably stay on the floor in the postseason given her offensive limitations? Can they survive extended stretches with Janelle Salaün at the 5? And how consistent will Williams be as a shooter?

Las Vegas might only have three players you can trust on any given night, but when those players are A'ja Wilson, Jackie Young and Chelsea Gray, and your coach is Becky Hammon, you're still going to win 30 regular-season games and be an absolute force to be reckoned with in the postseason.

Over their last 16 games since the All-Star break, Young is averaging 23.4 points and 6.6 assists on .50/.40/.90 shooting splits, while Wilson is averaging 25.8 points and 9.1 rebounds on 51.3 percent shooting from the field.

Not having NaLyssa Smith for the rest of the year due to a knee injury was a pretty big hit to their already poor depth. But if Young and Wilson continue to play at that level, there's a good chance they can elevate everyone around them to a serviceable level.

The Minnesota Lynx have been our No. 1 team all season, and nothing changes now. No other team is as elite in as many areas as the Lynx. They have tremendous pick-and-roll playmaking, shot creation, off-ball shooting, rim scoring and defense.

However, it's fair to have some concerns about this team entering the postseason. They've won just one of their last five games, with their lone victory coming in a game where they allowed 89 points to Connecticut.

There's no question Minnesota has peaked at the highest level of any team in the league on both ends of the floor this year. But can they get back to that level when it matters most?

articles.title: New NBA Rumors on Jalen Duren's Rare Weight Clause in Pistons' $200M Contract Offer
articles.summary: The Detroit Pistons' latest contract offer to restricted free-agent center Jalen Duren reportedly includes an uncommon weight clause.
articles.body:
The Detroit Pistons' latest contract offer to restricted free-agent center Jalen Duren reportedly includes an uncommon weight clause.

According to Hunter Patterson and Sam Amick of The Athletic, the Pistons have offered Duren a five-year, $200 million deal with the added caveat of a weight clause that would require Duren to weigh in monthly over the course of the year.

League sources indicated to Patterson and Amick that the weight clause would serve as an incentive in the contract rather than something that could result in it getting voided or lessened in base value.

Listed at 6'10" and 250 pounds, the 22-year-old Duren has long been viewed as a player who has a chiseled physique rather than a weight issue.

One league source even told Patterson and Amick that Duren "looks like a Greek statue."

The Pistons' concerns about Duren's weight reportedly came as a surprise to Duren and his representation during contract negotiations.

Per Patterson and Amick, Duren's struggles during the playoffs last season resulted in decision-makers within the Pistons' organization coming to the conclusion that they would prefer Duren to play at a lighter weight.

Selected 13th overall in the 2022 NBA draft out of Memphis, Duren enjoyed the best season of his young career in 2025-26, averaging a career-high 19.5 points per game on 65.0 percent shooting to go along with 10.5 rebounds and 2.0 assists.

Duren was named an All-Star and All-NBA Third Team selection for the first time as a result, but he did not perform at the same level come playoff time.

Appearing in 14 playoff contests for the top-seeded Pistons, Duren averaged 10.2 points on 51.4 percent shooting, plus 8.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists.

The Pistons were one of the NBA's biggest surprises last season, leading the Eastern Conference with a 60-22 record, but they fell short of the Eastern Conference Finals, losing in seven games to the Cleveland Cavaliers in the second round.

Duren's contract situation has been one of the biggest storylines throughout the offseason, but things have to come to a head soon since the Pistons are set to open training camp next week before beginning their regular-season schedule on Oct. 20.

According to Patterson and Amick, Duren is considering accepting his one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer prior to the Oct. 1 deadline since it would allow him to become an unrestricted free agent next offseason.

articles.title: Who was Lawrence Tanter? Los Angeles Lakers announcer passes away at 76, tributes pour in for the team’s legend

articles.body: The Los Angeles Lakers are mourning the death of longtime public address announcer Lawrence Tanter, who died at the age of 76. The team announced his passing on Wednesday night, bringing an end to the career of one of the most recognisable voices in Lakers history. Tanter was the voice of Lakers games for 43 years, from 1982 through 2026, and became a familiar presence for generations of fans at the arena.Tanter’s cause of death has not been revealed as of Thursday morning. The Chicago-born announcer had retired from his regular PA role in June after more than four decades with the franchise. However, he was expected to remain involved with the Lakers in game presentation work. His death comes months after he suffered a stroke in March.Who was Lawrence Tanter?Lawrence Tanter was born in Chicago in 1949. He later moved into radio and worked for a Southern California radio station during the 1970s. His career with the LA Lakers began in the early 1980s.He became the team’s public address announcer in 1982. Over the next 43 years, his booming voice became part of the Lakers’ identity. He announced games during some of the most memorable periods in franchise history. Tanter’s time behind the microphone, the Lakers won 10 NBA championships. He worked through different generations of players, coaches and fans. He also remained with the franchise through its move from the Staples Center era to the Crypto.com Arena era.The Lakers described Tanter as a cherished part of the organisation. articles.title: Florida Authorities Arrest NC State's Ex-Head Trainer Accused of Sex Abuse of Wolfpack Male Athletes
articles.summary: RALEIGH, N.C. (AP) — Authorities in Florida have arrested N.C. State's former director of sports medicine, who was accused of sexually abusing former Wolfpack male athletes under the guise of treatment, which previously led to more than 30 athletes outlining allegations in civil lawsuits.
articles.body:
RALEIGH, N.C. (AP) — Authorities in Florida have arrested N.C. State's former director of sports medicine, who was accused of sexually abusing former Wolfpack male athletes under the guise of treatment, which previously led to more than 30 athletes outlining allegations in civil lawsuits .

Robert M. Murphy Jr. was arrested Wednesday night and was being held in the Marion County jail on out-of-state fugitive warrants from North Carolina. The Marion County Sheriff's Office listed 23 charges of sexual battery and nine for felony sexual contact on its online database as of Thursday morning but offered no additional details.

Coach K's Son-in-Law, Former Assistant Dies at 47

ESPN was first to report Murphy's arrest.

Jared Hammett and Seth Blum, two Raleigh-based attorneys who have represented Murphy in the civil lawsuits, didn't immediately return an email from The Associated Press seeking comment.

The case originated with a federal civil lawsuit from a single athlete filed four years ago . That complaint alleged years of misconduct by Murphy, such as improper touching of the genitals during massages and intrusive observation while collecting urine samples during drug testing.

The case eventually landed in state court in 2025 with 14 former Wolfpack athletes, with that number growing to 31 joining the lawsuit by February outlining similar allegations.

In June, a judge dismissed the lawsuit against Murphy and multiple N.C. State athletics officials tied to their oversight roles, citing procedural reasons such as the statute of limitations expiring in claims dating back as early as 2013. Attorneys for the players had appealed that dismissal.

All but two of those 31 athletes were "John Doe" plaintiffs to protect their identity, while two former men's soccer players were named.

One is Benjamin Locke, who filed the original complaint in August 2022. The other is one of two athletes who filed their own federal lawsuits in February 2023 and April 2023 . The AP typically doesn't identify those who say they have been sexually assaulted or abused unless the person has spoken publicly about it, which Locke has done.

Durham-based attorney Kerry Sutton, who has represented players going back to the original case, told the AP that the number of athletes who have contacted players' attorneys with similar allegations has grown to 35.

Attorneys for Murphy have denied any wrongdoing by their client in previous comments. That notably included Blum forcefully defending his client after the lawsuit moved to state court last fall, saying Murphy had been falsely accused and there was yet to be "one scrap of credible evidence he assaulted anyone."

The judge's dismissal of the civil case in June had covered claims against multiple athletics officials, such as former athletic director Debbie Yow and current AD Boo Corrigan on jurisdictional grounds. That ruling stated any complaint should go through the North Carolina Industrial Commission — a state agency that deals with workplace matters because N.C. State is a public university — rather than civil court.

articles.title: Indiana Fever vs Minnesota Lynx season finale carries playoff seeding stakes for Caitlin Clark's team
articles.summary: Kelsey Mitchell set the WNBA single-season scoring record with 1,076 points as the Indiana Fever face the Minnesota Lynx in the regular season finale.
articles.body: We have reached the final day of the WNBA season. Regardless of if you follow it or not, the season has come and gone, and if you consume sports, you've probably heard about many of the main stories from the season. We've had Enes Kanter talk about wanting to declare himself eligible for the draft, more Caitlin Clark drama, injury storylines, and of course, the league seemingly shooting themselves in the foot. However, I want to focus on the good for this final day as the Fever take on the Lynx. The good for the Indiana Fever: Kelsey Mitchell. This has been a decent season for the Fever, but this team isn't trying to win the regular season; they are trying to win in the playoffs. We routinely see the Fever getting the best effort from their opponent because of the attention that comes when playing against Indiana. Part of the reason the Fever are so dangerous is that they have elite scorers at three positions. We all know how good Clark is, and the attention she commands. Even Aliyah Boston is recognized as a great talent as a former No. 1 pick. However, Kelsey Mitchell is the player who stands out the most to me with her scoring. She has increased her scoring each year for the past four seasons and is over 1,000 points for the year. As of tonight's game, she is at 1,076 points, setting the single-season record for most points in a season. This is just the third 1,000-point season in league history, and the first by someone other than A'ja Wilson. Mitchell doesn't even need to do most of the damage shooting from deep; she can score from all three levels. To her credit, she can shoot from three and has increased her made threes each year since 2020. CAITLIN CLARK RETURNS AFTER FIBA TITLE AS KELSEY MITCHELL SETS WNBA SCORING MARK IN FEVER VICTORY OVER TEMPO Over on the other side of the court, they have the Minnesota Lynx, with their good being Olivia Miles. The Lynx are already locked up with the #1 seed in the postseason, and normally you'd attribute that to Napheesa Collier. Last year, Collier was the MVP of the league and dominated for the Lynx. She got injured in the playoffs and only came back 15 games ago. Collier has been up to her old tricks, scoring in bunches and contributing a ton of rebounds. In 15 games this season, she is averaging 17.5 points and 6.9 rebounds. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The real story of this team is not Collier. Everyone expected the Lynx to step back because of Collier's injury. Instead, they drafted Olivia Miles, and, as the saying goes, the rich got richer. Miles has been simply fantastic for the Lynx. She is averaging almost 20 points per game for Minnesota in her first season and broke Clark's rookie points record. She is also averaging 4.7 rebounds and six assists. She is very efficient, too, shooting almost 50-40-90 from the key areas. articles.title: Jon Scheyer Addresses Duke Future After Turning Down Mavs HC Job, Cooper Flagg Reunion in NBA
articles.summary: After a successful start to his tenure at Duke, Jon Scheyer received some NBA interest, but ultimately remained in Durham.
articles.body:
After a successful start to his tenure at Duke, Jon Scheyer received some NBA interest, but ultimately remained in Durham.

Ahead of the 2026-27 season, Scheyer explained what kept him in his current role.

"I'm right where I'm supposed to be ... I'm in this for the long haul with Duke," Scheyer said at Duke Media Day.

Coach K's Son-in-Law, Former Assistant Dies at 47

After the Dallas Mavericks and Jason Kidd parted ways, the organization reportedly pursued Scheyer, and he had "major interest" in the job, according to Jeff Goodman of the Field of 68.

Despite his reported interest, Scheyer stayed at Duke, and the Mavs hired former Michigan coach Dusty May.

Scheyer said on the Glue Guys podcast (h/t The Athletic's Ira Gorawara ) that he "wouldn't be able to live with myself" if he left Duke without "seeing this through."

"I'm at a one-of-one place where not often you get your dream job when you're 33," Scheyer said. "And that's what happened to me."

Scheyer took over at Duke ahead of the 2022-23 campaign following the legendary Mike Krzyzewski's retirement. While he had big shoes to fill, he's arguably exceeded expectations so far, reaching the Elite Eight three times with one Final Four appearance.

"I'm really proud of the start we've gone off to and the continuation of what has been built here," Scheyer said. "But I think we've got so much left to do. We have so much left to accomplish."

Staying at the collegiate level means Scheyer will get to coach a roster built to win a championship rather than one that would be rebuilding at the NBA level.

The Blue Devils boast the No. 2 recruiting class in 2026, according to 247Sports . The group is highlighted by 5-star power forward Cameron Williams , the No. 4 player in the nation.

Scheyer had a whirlwind of an offseason as he weighed a potential job in the NBA against his current role, but he said the process "reenergized" and "refocused" him ahead of the 2026-27 campaign.

"In some ways, it made me even stronger in terms of my dedication and what we have to do here," Scheyer said. "I do think you want to double down on what you have to get right."

articles.title: NBA dark-horse contenders? Raptors, Warriors among teams that could make unexpected run
articles.summary: Here are five teams that maybe, just maybe could emerge as title threats this season.
articles.body:
Somehow, someway, we are only days away from the onslaught of media day and the opening of training camps in the NBA. A summer full of ideas, concepts, defensive schemes and drawn-up sets is closer to coming to fruition. Optimism can come and go, but this is the time of year where you can say the majority of teams are going to feel the most hopeful.

My mind starts to think about the contenders. Not just the Knicks , Spurs , and Thunders of the world, but the dark-horse contenders — the teams who believe they can make that leap. And whether it was last year's 60-win Pistons , the 64-win Cavaliers from two years ago, or the 51-win Grizzlies from 2022-23, someone always emerges.

And that's the beauty of basketball, it's not black and white, it's full of gray. No matter what it feels like, there truly is no one way to win. So here is my dice roll on some teams — whether they are already good and are being slept on, or that I think could get better throughout the season — that maybe, just maybe, just maybe could make a deep run in the playoffs.

It's not a gigantic surprise that a team featuring Kawhi Leonard may not only have championship aspirations but a route to get it done. He's quite literally done this in Toronto once before, and I'm not sure people get how much better the Raptors got over the course of last season. There's a reason they took Cleveland to seven games in the first round.

The regular season may have to get managed with Leonard, but his presence and self-creation should stabilize and elevate the Raptors in the half-court. His ability to draw the attention from the defense should pay dividends. I thought Brandon Ingram was great for the Raptors last year, but he had to make a lot of shots before defenses would blink. Not the same here.

Toronto can also offer different lineup combinations where RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickly have additional opportunities to shine (and they will be key). And none of what Kawhi does should disrupt or interrupt the continued growth of Scottie Barnes . Both can do a little bit of everything offensively and be moved around the board, attacking matchups and keeping pressure on teams in different ways.

The big key is going to be how much better this defense gets, not only in the regular season but in the playoffs. Having to deal with Leonard, Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles over the course of a playoff series does not seem like the most fun. The Raptors were already an active, physical group. Having ball pressure with Kawhi off-ball and able to either a) grizzly-bear swipe at drives or b) switch late in the shot clock could cause problems for offenses.

Yes, I can feel some version of a smirk through this screen, but hear me out. There is only one team that won two games against the New York Knicks during their playoff run, and that was the Hawks. Knicks fans have earned the right to play Empire State of Mind and N.Y. State of Mind and make as many rapper hand motions as they want, but CJ McCollum had them stressed out. That should not be lost to history.

The playoff questions are not going away, but the Hawks played offense with conviction: good pace and good tempo, and that became dangerous to deal with. When they get stops, opponents can find themselves caught playing their style, getting up and down the court, and, before they know it, there is a quick 10 points dropped on them.

Jalen Johnson improved last year, and part of why McCollum and Nickeil Alexander-Walker were so important was so that Johnson was not asked or required to make every play or read. What does this team look like if he gets better in that area? More drives, a greater ability to attack more matchups, more comfort scoring offensively overall. On the other end, adding Lu Dort 's experience is one thing, but having the ability to have him and Dyson Daniels playing defense at the same time is another.

But the real notion behind the Hawks making a run is the tale of two seasons they went through. Last season, they had Trae Young , they had Kristaps Porziņģis, and then they didn't. Then post-All-Star break, the Hawks went 20-6 and had the No. 2 defensive rating in the league. Could they have found a formula to sustain regular-season success with the knowledge of what they have to work on in the playoffs?

The Warriors haven't won a championship since 2021-22. They have finished outside of the top 4 in the West in five of the past six seasons. They missed out on the pursuit of LeBron James and did not make a splash move. I understand all of that. My counter?

I find it difficult to imagine Curry looking at the players they missed out on and not feeling a desire to go scorched earth. And that's all I need to envision to see how the Warriors could get it done. If he can stay healthy, time and time again he's shown he's more than able to make life hard on opponents. Should you live your life fueled by spite? Not really. Does it work more times than anyone wants to admit? Yes, it does.

Do we get a motivated Draymond Green ? Is Kristaps Porziņģis able to stay healthy? Does Yaxel Lendeborg fit right into what the Warriors like to do on both ends? Can Brandin Podziemski erase the memory of last year? Will Jimmy Butler get healthy at just the right time and bring all of his playoff rising to the table? The power of continuity may not be the Warriors' strength, but at some point it has to pay off, right? RIGHT?

Health will be the ultimate factor for the Warriors. They started 10-2 in 2024-25, and 4-1 in '25-26. The issue has been sustaining success on top of staying healthy. If the Warriors can win enough games to break out of the pack and hover around the top 4-5 in the West, they can make a run.

I know it feels a little odd to take a team that won 19 games and throw it into the title race. However: Gap years can tend to work out and Tyrese Haliburton is back. So Pacers fans, start your engines, am I right?

The intrigue here is not just the return of Haliburton. It will likely take time, which may throw off expectations, but we've seen how impactful Haliburton can be to the Pacers' formula for success. And that's the point: We've seen the Pacers perform at a high enough level to knock on the door of a championship. Some may feel that wasn't sustainable, but the Pacers proved difficult to deal with.

Offensively, it was not just how fast they played, it was how many actions they got to and how much pressure they put on you. Seeing how Ivica Zubac fits into that as a screener, roller and playmaker should be fun. There is also an argument Zubac will be stronger on the defensive end and help anchor things now that the shock of going to the Pacers midseason has worn off.

Lineup versatility and depth have been a hallmark of the best Pacers runs. Pascal Siakam continues to be a fearless scorer who has consistently fit right in with what the Pacers want to do, and offseason acquisition Kelly Oubre Jr. also adds to what Andrew Nembhard , Aaron Nesmith and Ben Sheppard have provided.

Rick Carlisle has proven he knows what these Pacers are, what they need and how to allow them to work to get there. If it's all systems are go and they learn the lessons from the lumps of last year, why wouldn't we imagine Haliburton eventually getting right back to the position he was at before the injury? And if he does that, you're going to have to deal with the Pacers.

The Magic have dealt with three consecutive first-round exits. But last year there were attempts and moments that once again reminded us what the Magic formula could be, including a trip to the NBA Cup semis and a 10-4 record in November with the No. 7 offensive rating and the No. 4 defensive rating.

You could easily point to the injury button to explain their drop-off, and that would be fair. You would also have to point to the fact that the pace and tempo slowed over the course of the season, though, and their defense … stopped defending.

Enter Sean Sweeney, who has been a key part of building defenses in Dallas and San Antonio (among other stops in his career). Could a return to form on that end build on the tough time the Magic gave the Pistons in the first round? We've seen what this team can accomplish when they do defend, but the hope isn't just a return to guarding but implementing a stronger offense.

Sometimes big trades and big swings feel and look better in Year 2. Do we see a stronger effort from Desmond Bane ? There's been discussion about the combination of Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner , but we've seen talented, young wings figure out how to mesh in the Eastern Conference before. If Banchero can deliver even more drives, and if Wagner can stay healthy and maintain confidence on offense, is there more potential than we think? Nikola Vučević came back home for a reason; spacing the floor is one thing, but can his post-ups and handoff work also boost some second units?

Work has to be done, but if they can hit the right notes, the Magic may not be a team you want to see in the playoffs.

articles.title: Hurricanes star Malik Reneau returning to UM after court grants eligibility
articles.summary: The Miami Hurricanes’ basketball team got a huge boost on Thursday. Malik Reneau, UM’s All-ACC forward who helped lead them back to the NCAA Tournament last...
articles.body:
The Miami Hurricanes' basketball team got a huge boost on Thursday.

Malik Reneau, UM's All-ACC forward who helped lead them back to the NCAA Tournament last season, received another year of eligibility after an Indiana judge granted an injunction against the NCAA, allowing Reneau and other college players to return to their teams.

The NCAA is expected to appeal the court decision, according to ESPN. The Hurricanes announced Reneau's return on social media.

Reneau has been practicing with the Hurricanes while his status was in limbo.

"It's just day by day. Malik is going day by day, and we're just trying to figure out what's next and if he will be able to play or if (he) will be in shape to go somewhere else and continue his professional career," Miami coach Jai Lucas said Monday. "… We really don't have any answers. I don't have any answers. I don't think anybody does. But he's here and he's been practicing and participating. He's in school. And so we're just working towards that … We're operating as if he would be a part of the team."

Reneau's return gives the retooled Hurricanes another key player for Lucas' second year at the helm in Coral Gables.

Reneau, a 6-foot-9, 235-pound forward and Miami native, transferred from Indiana to UM before the 2025-26 season. He excelled with the Hurricanes, averaging 18.9 points and 6.5 rebounds.

Reneau went undrafted in this year's NBA draft, and he signed an Exhibit 10 contract with the Orlando Magic.

Miami returns three other players from last year's tournament team: Marcus Allen, Dante Allen and Shelton Henderson. Marcus Allen is out for the season after suffering a torn ACL .

Reneau joins a team that added multiple key transfers, including Villanova guard Acaden Lewis and Georgia center Somto Cyril. UM also signed five-star Miami Columbus forward Caleb Gaskins.

Dozens of athletes have sued the NCAA for eligibility after the organization implemented a "Five-for-Five" age-based eligibility model, which gives student-athletes five years to play in up to five seasons in college.

"t's weird. Completely weird. It's like Twilight Zone, you know what I mean?" Lucas said. "We just don't know anything. You don't know NIL. You don't know what next year looks like. You don't know if fifth-years are going to play. You don't know about internationals. It's just a bunch of questions and a bunch of unknowns that you're just trying to adapt to, and you're just trying to wait till you get some type of direction of where things are going. And until then, we're kind of just figuring out what's next."

articles.title: Wizards GM Talks Anthony Davis Contract, Hypes Deandre Ayton, Backs HC Keefe Ahead of NBA Season
articles.summary: As one of the most fascinating teams entering the 2026-27 season because of their range of outcomes, Washington Wizards general manager Will Dawkins met with the media on Thursday to discuss their outlook.
articles.body:
As one of the most fascinating teams entering the 2026-27 season because of their range of outcomes, Washington Wizards general manager Will Dawkins met with the media on Thursday to discuss their outlook.

The biggest topic was Anthony Davis not getting a contract extension, at least thus far, but Dawkins expressed no concern about the 10-time All-Star being able to "remind the basketball world who he is."

Dawkins also had positive things to say about the addition of Deandre Ayton, who he called a "starting level center and probably the best backup in the league."

With the Wizards heading into a new era, head coach Brian Keefe is in uncharted territory going into his fourth season after putting together a 43-160 record since taking over midway through the 2023-24 season following Wes Unseld Jr.'s firing.

Dawkins threw his "full confidence" behind Keefe being able to get the Wizards to take a step forward.

One thing that will help Keefe and the Wizards is the return of Alex Sarr, who missed 34 games last season due in part to a toe injury and underwent surgery in June to repair a fractured foot suffered during an offseason workout.

Dawkins said the team anticipates Sarr being ready for opening night, but he will open training camp in a limited capacity.

Davis' contract has been a focal point since the Wizards acquired him from the Dallas Mavericks in February. He didn't appear in a game with Washington after the trade and is entering the final guaranteed year of his current contract with a $58.5 million salary.

The deal also includes a $62.8 million player option for 2027-28, but Davis has been eligible to sign an extension for up to four years and $275 million since Aug. 6.

However, the two sides have reportedly agreed to hold off any contract talks until after the season starts.

Washington also acquired Ayton in the offseason to provide more frontcourt depth if Davis misses time. The 28-year-old had a solid 2025-26 campaign with the Los Angeles Lakers, averaging 12.5 points and 8.0 rebounds per game in 72 starts.

Considering Davis has played fewer than 60 games in five of the last six seasons, someone like Ayton offers the Wizards some insurance if he has to take on a bigger role.

Keefe's status is worth monitoring because he has the second-worst winning percentage in NBA history with at least 150 games as a head coach. Much of that lack of success is not his fault because the Wizards weren't set up to compete.

Things look very different for the Wizards going into 2026-27 with a potential starting five featuring Davis, Sarr, Trae Young, AJ Dybantsa and Kyshawn George.

That's not a bad unit to work with when everyone is healthy. Dybantsa, the No. 1 pick in the 2026 draft, and his development is the most important thing for the Wizards this season.

If Davis and Young get back to their All-Star form, there's a world in which the Wizards are competing for a playoff spot in the Eastern Conference. That would be huge progress for a franchise that has won a total of 50 games over the past three seasons.
